claims.text: The as-sprayed FeNiCrCoCu coating has a relatively coarse as-deposited microstructure without significant nanotwinning or oxide stabilization.
Vacuum heat treatment at about 500 °C induces recrystallized nanograins in the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
Vacuum heat treatment at about 500 °C induces a nanotwin-rich heterogeneous microstructure.
The 500 °C vacuum treatment enables formation of a limited, adherent protective oxide on the coating surface.
A 500 °C vacuum heat treatment produces the highest microhardness and improved wear resistance relative to other reported heat-treatment conditions.
The nanotwin-rich nanocrystalline structure is responsible for the increase in microhardness.
The hardened microstructure resists crack initiation and coating spallation during wear.
Controlled recrystallization and nanoscale-twin formation increase dislocation density.
The induced nanoscale twins hinder plastic deformation during sliding contact.
A stable, potentially chromium-rich oxide scale slows oxidative wear.
Higher coating hardness improves resistance to abrasive and fatigue wear.
The combined nanotwin-hardening and protective-oxide effects improve resistance to adhesive and abrasive wear at high temperature.
Relative to the as-sprayed coating, the 500 °C vacuum-treated coating will have significantly greater microhardness.
Relative to the as-sprayed coating, the 500 °C vacuum-treated coating will have a lower wear rate during sliding wear conducted at 500 °C.
The heat-treated coating will show less spallation than the as-sprayed coating.
The heat-treated coating will show fewer oxide-induced crack propagations than the as-sprayed coating.
The proposed mechanism applies to sliding wear between approximately 500 and 700 °C under high normal load and sliding speed.
At 700 and 900 °C heat-treatment conditions, decreased hardness is associated with intensified abrasive wear, crack expansion, and coating peeling.
The relative contributions of hardness increase and oxide-scale lubrication to wear reduction are not yet quantified.
Failure to obtain a significant hardness increase with a corresponding wear-rate reduction, or observation of increased spallation and cracking, would falsify the hypothesis.
